query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor doping level of boron to refractory high‐entropy alloys (e.g. HfMoNbTaTiZr) will improve ductility and promote more uniform deformation by precipitating fine boride phases at the grain boundaries, which enhance intergranular cohesion, while maintaining or slightly enhancing high strength and preserving impact‐induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory high‐entropy alloy (such as an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr with a disordered BCC solid-solution structure) that in its untreated state shows limited ductility with predominant intergranular fracture under dynamic loading.
generation.intervention: A minor addition of boron during alloy synthesis to promote intergranular boride precipitation.
generation.conditions: Testing under both quasi‑static and dynamic (impact-relevant, high strain rate) loading conditions at room temperature and elevated temperatures; the alloy is processed by conventional vacuum-arc melting or similar methods ensuring a homogeneous distribution of the minor boron addition.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitated fine boride phases forming at the grain boundaries that enhance intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: The boron addition segregates at the grain boundaries where it reacts to form fine boride precipitates, thereby reinforcing the boundaries by increasing their cohesion and delaying intergranular cracking. This mediation of the deformation leads to a transition toward more transgranular fracture modes, which supports both high strength and rapid impact-induced energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a significant improvement in uniform elongation (e.g., an increase in fracture strain from around 12% to about 19–20%), a moderate enhancement in ultimate compressive strength, and sustained energetic performance under dynamic impact. The yield strength is anticipated to remain similar or show a slight increase relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys without boron, which typically show lower work hardenability and primarily intergranular fracture leading to reduced ductility under dynamic loading, though they already possess high strength and notable energy release characteristics.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold for alloys that form a disordered BCC matrix and are amenable to boride precipitation at the grain boundaries; excessive boron or different alloy chemistries may lead to the formation of coarse, brittle intermetallic phases that could compromise both ductility and energy release.
generation.uncertainty: While the evidence supports improved work hardenability and ductility via grain-boundary strengthening in similar systems, the direct influence on impact-induced energy release remains less quantified. The balance between ductility improvement and preserving energetic performance under extreme dynamic conditions requires precise control of boron content and uniform precipitation, and slight variations in processing may affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical processing conditions: one set using the standard HfMoNbTaTiZr composition (control) and another with an added 0.1 at.% boron. Characterize both sets by detailed microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to verify the presence and distribution of boride precipitates. Then, subject both sets to quasi‐static and dynamic compression/tensile tests as well as impact tests (using high-speed imaging and energy-release measurements).
measurements: Fracture strain and uniform elongation from mechanical testing
Yield and ultimate strengths (compressive and tensile)
Microstructural characterization of grain boundary phases
Quantitative assessments of energy-release behavior (e.g., reaction delay time, maximum energy release intensity) during high strain rate impact tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase (e.g., ≥20% relative improvement) in fracture strain and uniform plastic deformation compared to the control, or if any observed improvement in ductility is accompanied by a ≥10% reduction in yield/ultimate strength or a measurable deterioration in impact-induced energy release performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.

An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.
